ONE FILE · SIX LEARNING VIEWS

DevOps & DevSecOps pipeline — Beginner, Intermediate and Advanced

A white-themed learning portal that keeps the same eight-stage delivery flow but explains it at three experience levels. It also separates the DevOps view from the DevSecOps view, uses one small example project throughout, and shows how infrastructure provisioning plus application deployment changes across VMs, managed/on-prem Kubernetes, serverless and PaaS targets.

DevOps: 3 levelsDevSecOps: 3 levels8-stage flowTerraform + Ansible + KubernetesVM + Serverless + PaaSStandalone HTML

Choose DevOps

Learn the mechanics of planning, building, testing, packaging, releasing, deploying and operating software.

BeginnerLearn the loopIntermediateAutomate environmentsAdvancedEngineer the platform

Choose DevSecOps

Learn the same flow with security, supply-chain and compliance controls embedded at every stage.

BeginnerAdd basic securityIntermediateBuild security gatesAdvancedSecure the factory
How to use this portal
Start with your current level. Read the eight stages in order once. Then use the deployment-target and tool-glossary sections as references. You do not need to learn every tool at once; learn the responsibility first, then one tool that fulfills it.

Example project used in all six views: TaskPulse

TaskPulse is intentionally small so the delivery concepts stay visible. It has a browser frontend, REST API and database. The deployment mechanics can change without changing the core application.

BrowserReact UI
→
APIFastAPI
→
DatabasePostgreSQL

Repositories

taskpulse/
  app/frontend/
  app/api/
  tests/
  Dockerfile
  deploy/helm/
  deploy/ansible/
  infra/terraform/
  .ci/

One application, many targets

  • VM: Terraform + Ansible.
  • Kubernetes: Terraform + Helm/Kustomize + optional Argo CD.
  • Serverless function: a smaller API handler package + Terraform.
  • Serverless container: same OCI image + Cloud Run/Container Apps/App Runner/Fargate.
  • Static UI: frontend bundle + object storage/CDN.

Original DevSecOps reference diagram

The six learning views below preserve this Plan → Code → Build → Test → Package → Release → Deploy → Operate & Monitor mental model. The DevOps views emphasize delivery and reliability; the DevSecOps views additionally surface security activities and evidence.

DevOpsBeginner

DevOps — Beginner

For someone new to DevOps. The objective is to understand the delivery loop and successfully ship a small application without being overwhelmed by enterprise terminology.

1. PlanUnderstand the work before changing code.2. CodeImplement the change in version control.3. BuildTurn source into a repeatable build output.4. TestProve the change works and meets quality expectations.5. PackageCreate an immutable deployable artifact.6. ReleaseApprove and promote a known version.7. DeployPut infrastructure and application into an environment.8. Operate & MonitorRun, observe, support and improve the service.

What you should be able to do

  • Explain the eight stages in plain language.
  • Use Git and a pull request.
  • Run a basic CI build/test pipeline.
  • Create a container image.
  • Provision one simple target with Terraform.
  • Deploy to a VM, Kubernetes or a serverless platform.
  • Read logs and a dashboard.

Hands-on project for this level

TaskPulse Lite: React UI + FastAPI API + SQLite/PostgreSQL.

  1. Run locally.
  2. Put code in Git.
  3. Create one CI pipeline that builds and tests.
  4. Build a Docker image.
  5. Deploy first to one Linux VM.
  6. Then repeat the deployment to a local Kubernetes cluster or one serverless target.
1
STAGE 1

Plan

Decide what you are building and what “done” means.

Key activities
  • Write a small user story and acceptance criteria.
  • Break the work into a few tasks.
  • Decide the target environment: local, VM, Kubernetes or serverless.
Tools and how they are used
  • Jira — track the story, task, owner and status
  • Confluence — write a short design note, runbook or decision
  • GitHub/GitLab Issues — a lighter alternative to Jira for backlog tracking
What leaves the stage
  • User story
  • Acceptance criteria
  • Very small architecture sketch
TaskPulse example

Create story TP-1: “As a user I can create a task.” Acceptance: POST /tasks returns 201 and the task appears in the UI.

2
STAGE 2

Code

Make the smallest change in Git and have somebody review it.

Key activities
  • Create a branch.
  • Write or change application code.
  • Run the application locally.
  • Open a pull/merge request.
Tools and how they are used
  • Git — record changes and history
  • GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket — host repositories and perform pull/merge reviews
  • VS Code or IDE — write and debug code
What leaves the stage
  • Source code commit
  • Pull/merge request
  • Review comments
TaskPulse example

Add a FastAPI POST /tasks endpoint, commit it on feature/create-task, then open a merge request.

3
STAGE 3

Build

Prove the source can be converted into something runnable in the same way every time.

Key activities
  • Install dependencies from a lock file.
  • Compile/bundle if required.
  • Create a clean build directory.
Tools and how they are used
  • npm / yarn — install and bundle the React frontend
  • Maven / Gradle — build Java applications when the backend is Java
  • pip / Poetry — install Python dependencies for the FastAPI example
What leaves the stage
  • Frontend dist/ directory
  • Backend package or runnable source bundle
  • Build log
TaskPulse example

Run npm ci && npm run build for the UI and pip install -r requirements.txt for the API.

4
STAGE 4

Test

Run automated checks before packaging.

Key activities
  • Run unit tests.
  • Run a small API/integration test.
  • Fail the pipeline when tests fail.
Tools and how they are used
  • PyTest — test Python functions and FastAPI endpoints
  • JUnit — test Java code
  • CI runner — execute tests automatically on every merge request
What leaves the stage
  • Test report
  • Pass/fail result
TaskPulse example

PyTest calls POST /tasks and GET /tasks using a test database.

5
STAGE 5

Package

Put the application into a versioned artifact that can be moved to another environment.

Key activities
  • Build a Docker image or zip/binary.
  • Give the artifact a unique version.
  • Push it to a repository/registry.
Tools and how they are used
  • Docker / BuildKit — build the application container image
  • ECR / ACR / Artifact Registry — store container images
  • Nexus / Artifactory — store binaries and language packages
What leaves the stage
  • taskpulse-api:1.0.0 image
  • taskpulse-ui:1.0.0 image or frontend bundle
TaskPulse example

Build taskpulse-api:1.0.0 and push it to your registry.

6
STAGE 6

Release

Choose which tested version is allowed to go to an environment.

Key activities
  • Create a release/version.
  • Record release notes.
  • Approve production when required.
Tools and how they are used
  • Git tag/release — mark the exact commit
  • Jenkins / GitLab CI / GitHub Actions — pause for an approval and promote the selected version
  • Change record — record what is changing in controlled environments
What leaves the stage
  • Release 1.0.0
  • Approved artifact version
  • Release notes
TaskPulse example

Tag v1.0.0 and approve that exact image digest for staging.

7
STAGE 7

Deploy

Provision the target infrastructure and install the application.

Key activities
  • Create or update infrastructure.
  • Deploy the application.
  • Run a health check.
Tools and how they are used
  • Terraform — provision VM, network, load balancer, Kubernetes cluster or serverless resources
  • Ansible — configure VMs and install services
  • Helm — install a containerized app into Kubernetes
  • Cloud CLI/provider action — update a serverless function or managed app service
What leaves the stage
  • Running environment
  • Deployment log
  • Health-check result
TaskPulse example

VM: Terraform creates EC2, Ansible installs Docker and runs the image. Kubernetes: Terraform creates EKS, Helm deploys the image. Serverless: Terraform creates Lambda and deploys the function package.

8
STAGE 8

Operate & Monitor

Know whether the service is healthy and learn from problems.

Key activities
  • Watch logs and basic metrics.
  • Create one availability alert.
  • Fix incidents and add follow-up work to the backlog.
Tools and how they are used
  • Prometheus — collect application and infrastructure metrics
  • Grafana — display dashboards and alerts
  • ELK / Splunk — centralize and search logs
  • Cloud-native monitoring — CloudWatch / Azure Monitor / Cloud Monitoring for provider resources
What leaves the stage
  • Dashboard
  • Alert
  • Incident notes
  • Improvement ticket
TaskPulse example

Dashboard request count, latency and error rate. Create an alert when 5xx errors exceed the agreed threshold.

DevOpsIntermediate

DevOps — Intermediate

For engineers who already use Git, CI and containers. The focus shifts to repeatability, environment promotion, IaC, multiple deployment targets and operability.

1. PlanUnderstand the work before changing code.2. CodeImplement the change in version control.3. BuildTurn source into a repeatable build output.4. TestProve the change works and meets quality expectations.5. PackageCreate an immutable deployable artifact.6. ReleaseApprove and promote a known version.7. DeployPut infrastructure and application into an environment.8. Operate & MonitorRun, observe, support and improve the service.

What you should be able to do

  • Design dev/staging/prod promotion.
  • Build once and promote immutable artifacts.
  • Use Terraform, Ansible and Helm appropriately.
  • Add integration/performance validation.
  • Implement rollback and observable releases.
  • Choose the right deployment model for VM, Kubernetes or serverless.

Hands-on project for this level

TaskPulse Staged: React + FastAPI + PostgreSQL with dev/staging/prod.

  1. Provision infrastructure with Terraform.
  2. Use Ansible for VM deployment and Helm for Kubernetes.
  3. Store images by digest in a registry.
  4. Add automated integration tests.
  5. Add dashboards, release approvals and rollback.
1
STAGE 1

Plan

Turn requirements into deployable, observable work.

Key activities
  • Refine stories and non-functional requirements.
  • Define environments and promotion path.
  • Record architecture decisions and rollback expectations.
  • Define SLI/SLO candidates.
Tools and how they are used
  • Jira — epics, stories, dependencies and release scope
  • Confluence — ADR, operational requirements and runbooks
  • Backstage/service catalog — optional ownership and service metadata
What leaves the stage
  • Traceable backlog
  • ADR
  • Environment/release plan
  • Initial SLO
TaskPulse example

TaskPulse defines dev → staging → prod, 99.9% API availability, PostgreSQL backup requirement and rollback to the prior image digest.

2
STAGE 2

Code

Use a controlled Git workflow with automated feedback.

Key activities
  • Short-lived branches or trunk-based development.
  • Required PR review.
  • Formatting/linting and pre-commit checks.
  • Version application and infrastructure code together or via linked repositories.
Tools and how they are used
  • GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket — branch protection, reviews, status checks
  • pre-commit — run repeatable local checks
  • SonarLint — developer feedback on code quality
  • CODEOWNERS — route reviews to accountable teams
What leaves the stage
  • Reviewed PR
  • Commit SHA
  • Linked infrastructure/config change
TaskPulse example

A PR updates FastAPI code, Terraform variable defaults and Helm values; required checks must pass before merge.

3
STAGE 3

Build

Create deterministic outputs and reuse caches safely.

Key activities
  • Use locked dependency versions.
  • Build in clean ephemeral runners.
  • Cache dependencies without caching mutable build output.
  • Stamp build metadata with commit SHA/version.
Tools and how they are used
  • BuildKit — layer-cached reproducible container builds
  • Maven/Gradle/npm/yarn — language builds using lock files
  • Jenkins/GitLab CI/GitHub Actions — ephemeral orchestration and artifact passing
What leaves the stage
  • Versioned binaries/images
  • Build metadata
  • Dependency manifest
TaskPulse example

CI builds frontend and API images labeled with git SHA, then exports image digests to later jobs.

4
STAGE 4

Test

Use a test pyramid and environment-level validation.

Key activities
  • Unit tests.
  • Integration tests with ephemeral dependencies.
  • Contract/API tests.
  • Smoke test the deployable image.
  • Optional performance baseline.
Tools and how they are used
  • PyTest/JUnit — unit and integration tests
  • Docker Compose/Testcontainers — spin up PostgreSQL or dependencies for tests
  • Postman/Newman or REST test suite — API contract tests
  • k6/JMeter — basic load test where useful
What leaves the stage
  • Unit/integration reports
  • Coverage trend
  • Smoke test result
  • Performance baseline
TaskPulse example

CI launches PostgreSQL, runs PyTest, starts the API container and checks /health and CRUD flows.

5
STAGE 5

Package

Produce immutable deployables for multiple targets.

Key activities
  • Build OCI images and/or machine packages.
  • Push once to an artifact repository.
  • Use immutable digests and retention rules.
Tools and how they are used
  • Docker/BuildKit — OCI image creation
  • ECR/ACR/Artifact Registry — image storage
  • Nexus/Artifactory — deb/rpm/zip/jar/package storage
What leaves the stage
  • Image digest
  • Binary checksum
  • Promotion metadata
TaskPulse example

The API image is pushed once. Staging and production both use sha256:… rather than rebuilding.

6
STAGE 6

Release

Promote artifacts using environment policies.

Key activities
  • Automate dev/staging promotion.
  • Require production approval only where risk requires it.
  • Generate changelog from commits/PRs.
  • Define rollback procedure.
Tools and how they are used
  • CI/CD platform environments — environment protection and approvals
  • Git tags/releases — version marker
  • ITSM/change system — change evidence for controlled production
What leaves the stage
  • Approved release candidate
  • Release notes
  • Rollback version
TaskPulse example

Staging auto-deploys; production requires an approval that points to the already-tested digest.

7
STAGE 7

Deploy

Treat infrastructure and application deployment as code.

Key activities
  • Terraform plan/apply for target resources.
  • Separate infrastructure lifecycle from frequent app releases where practical.
  • Use Ansible for VM configuration.
  • Use Helm/Kustomize and optionally Argo CD for Kubernetes.
  • Use deployment slots/revisions/aliases for managed/serverless platforms.
Tools and how they are used
  • Terraform — IaC plan and apply
  • Ansible — idempotent VM configuration and rolling deployment
  • Helm/Kustomize — Kubernetes manifests
  • Argo CD — GitOps reconciliation
  • Cloud deployment mechanisms — Lambda aliases, Cloud Run revisions, App Service slots
What leaves the stage
  • Terraform plan
  • Deployment revision
  • Health evidence
  • Rollback target
TaskPulse example

The same release can target an EC2 Auto Scaling group via Ansible, an EKS cluster via Argo CD, or Lambda via Terraform + alias promotion.

8
STAGE 8

Operate & Monitor

Operate against service objectives, not only host health.

Key activities
  • Define RED/USE dashboards.
  • Centralize logs and traces.
  • Create actionable alerts with runbooks.
  • Track deployment version in telemetry.
  • Run post-incident review.
Tools and how they are used
  • Prometheus — metrics and alert rules
  • Grafana — dashboards
  • ELK/Splunk — logs and searches
  • OpenTelemetry — portable traces/metrics/log context
  • Pager/incident tooling — route actionable alerts
What leaves the stage
  • SLO dashboard
  • Alert rules
  • Runbook
  • Post-incident actions
TaskPulse example

Every log contains service, environment, version and trace_id so incidents can be tied back to a release.

Intermediate pipeline skeleton

on: pull_request / main

PR pipeline:
  1. checkout
  2. install from lock files
  3. lint + unit tests
  4. build application
  5. integration tests
  6. terraform fmt/validate/plan (when IaC changed)

main/release pipeline:
  1. build image once
  2. push image and record digest
  3. deploy to staging
  4. smoke/integration validation
  5. approval if production policy requires it
  6. deploy the SAME digest to production
  7. annotate monitoring with release version
DevOpsAdvanced

DevOps — Advanced

For platform, SRE and senior DevOps engineers. The focus is scalable software delivery architecture, progressive delivery, multi-environment governance, hybrid targets and measurable engineering performance.

1. PlanUnderstand the work before changing code.2. CodeImplement the change in version control.3. BuildTurn source into a repeatable build output.4. TestProve the change works and meets quality expectations.5. PackageCreate an immutable deployable artifact.6. ReleaseApprove and promote a known version.7. DeployPut infrastructure and application into an environment.8. Operate & MonitorRun, observe, support and improve the service.

What you should be able to do

  • Design reusable delivery platforms instead of one-off pipelines.
  • Use GitOps/progressive delivery and feature flags.
  • Operate multi-region or hybrid deployment patterns.
  • Apply SLO/error-budget thinking.
  • Measure DORA and platform effectiveness.
  • Reduce toil through paved roads and reusable modules.

Hands-on project for this level

TaskPulse Platform: reusable multi-target delivery.

  1. Reusable Terraform modules for VM, Kubernetes and serverless containers.
  2. GitOps for Kubernetes.
  3. Progressive delivery and feature flags.
  4. Multi-region or hybrid target.
  5. SLO/error-budget-driven operations and DORA metrics.
1
STAGE 1

Plan

Design for operability, multi-environment delivery and failure.

Key activities
  • Map business capability to services and ownership.
  • Define SLO/error budget, RTO/RPO and capacity assumptions.
  • Decide deployment topology and data migration strategy.
  • Model multi-region or hybrid constraints.
Tools and how they are used
  • Jira/portfolio tooling — release trains, cross-team dependencies, risk
  • Confluence/ADR repository — architecture and operational decisions
  • Service catalog — ownership, dependencies, tier, SLO and runbook metadata
What leaves the stage
  • Architecture decision set
  • SLO/RTO/RPO
  • Deployment strategy
  • Dependency map
TaskPulse example

TaskPulse is classified tier-2, 99.9% SLO, RTO 60 minutes, RPO 15 minutes; API is stateless and deployable to VM, Kubernetes or serverless containers.

2
STAGE 2

Code

Optimize for high-frequency integration and strong repository governance.

Key activities
  • Trunk-based development with feature flags.
  • Required status checks and CODEOWNERS.
  • Automated versioning/changelog.
  • Reusable pipeline components.
  • Infrastructure modules with semantic versioning.
Tools and how they are used
  • GitHub/GitLab — merge queues, protected environments, OIDC to cloud
  • Feature flag platform — decouple deployment from release
  • pre-commit/linters — fast deterministic local feedback
  • Module registries — controlled Terraform/Helm reuse
What leaves the stage
  • Traceable commit
  • Reusable module changes
  • Feature flag state
TaskPulse example

A backward-compatible database migration lands before application code; the feature is disabled until production verification.

3
STAGE 3

Build

Create hermetic, scalable and attestable build outputs.

Key activities
  • Ephemeral isolated runners.
  • Pinned toolchain/container images.
  • Remote build caching with trust boundaries.
  • Cross-platform/multi-arch builds.
  • Build metadata/attestation.
Tools and how they are used
  • BuildKit/buildx — multi-platform OCI build
  • Bazel/Gradle build cache — large-scale deterministic caching where applicable
  • CI OIDC — short-lived cloud access
  • Artifact repository — promote, retain and replicate
What leaves the stage
  • Multi-arch image digests
  • Build attestation
  • Toolchain metadata
TaskPulse example

linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 images are built once and pushed under one manifest list, enabling x86 VMs and ARM Kubernetes nodes.

4
STAGE 4

Test

Use risk-based progressive validation.

Key activities
  • Parallel unit/integration/contract suites.
  • Ephemeral environment tests.
  • Database migration validation.
  • Performance/regression tests.
  • Chaos/resilience tests for critical paths.
Tools and how they are used
  • PyTest/JUnit — fast correctness tests
  • Testcontainers — ephemeral dependencies
  • k6/Gatling/JMeter — performance
  • Chaos Mesh/Litmus — Kubernetes resilience testing where justified
What leaves the stage
  • Quality gates
  • Performance envelope
  • Resilience evidence
  • Migration validation
TaskPulse example

A preview environment is created per PR for integration tests, then destroyed automatically.

5
STAGE 5

Package

Manage artifacts as the promotion unit across environments and regions.

Key activities
  • Immutable artifact promotion.
  • Repository replication and retention policies.
  • Base image strategy.
  • Separate config from artifacts.
Tools and how they are used
  • ECR/ACR/Artifact Registry — regional replication and lifecycle
  • Nexus/Artifactory — binary promotion channels
  • Packer — optional machine image creation for immutable VM deployments
What leaves the stage
  • Promotion-ready artifact
  • Regional replicas
  • Machine image/image digest
TaskPulse example

VM deployments can use a baked AMI built by Packer while Kubernetes and Cloud Run use the same application container digest.

6
STAGE 6

Release

Use progressive delivery and automated guardrails.

Key activities
  • Canary, blue/green or ring promotion.
  • Automated rollback based on SLO indicators.
  • Feature flag activation separate from deployment.
  • Change evidence generated from pipeline.
Tools and how they are used
  • Argo Rollouts/Flagger — progressive Kubernetes delivery
  • Cloud load balancer/traffic manager — weighted VM/serverless traffic
  • Feature flags — business rollout
  • CI/CD environments — release authorization
What leaves the stage
  • Traffic policy
  • Automated rollback rule
  • Release evidence
TaskPulse example

5% → 25% → 100% traffic is shifted only if error rate and p95 latency remain within thresholds.

7
STAGE 7

Deploy

Run platform-independent delivery patterns across hybrid targets.

Key activities
  • Terraform remote state, locking and module governance.
  • Golden-image or configuration-as-code VM strategy.
  • GitOps for Kubernetes.
  • Cross-account/subscription/project identity federation.
  • Multi-region deployment and disaster recovery.
Tools and how they are used
  • Terraform/Terragrunt — multi-environment IaC orchestration
  • Ansible — configuration where mutable hosts remain
  • Argo CD — Kubernetes reconciliation at scale
  • Helm/Kustomize — application packaging
  • Packer — immutable VM image pipelines
What leaves the stage
  • Environment state
  • Drift report
  • Deployment revision
  • DR readiness
TaskPulse example

Prod can span an EKS primary region, a warm VM fallback pool and an on-prem Kubernetes cluster, while deployment metadata remains tied to one release version.

8
STAGE 8

Operate & Monitor

Close the delivery loop with platform engineering and SRE practices.

Key activities
  • SLOs and error budgets.
  • Service-level telemetry with exemplars/traces.
  • Automated remediation where safe.
  • Capacity/cost observability.
  • Continuous improvement from incidents and delivery metrics.
Tools and how they are used
  • Prometheus/Grafana — service and platform observability
  • OpenTelemetry — vendor-neutral traces and telemetry context
  • ELK/Splunk — large-scale log analysis
  • FinOps tooling — cost attribution and optimization
  • DORA metrics — measure delivery performance
What leaves the stage
  • SLO/error budget
  • MTTR and DORA trends
  • Capacity plan
  • Improvement backlog
TaskPulse example

Deployments are annotated on dashboards; rollback automation can trigger when the release burns the error budget too quickly.

DevSecOpsBeginner

DevSecOps — Beginner

For someone learning how security fits into DevOps. Security is introduced as small checks and secure defaults at every stage rather than as a separate final review.

1. PlanUnderstand the work before changing code.2. CodeImplement the change in version control.3. BuildTurn source into a repeatable build output.4. TestProve the change works and meets quality expectations.5. PackageCreate an immutable deployable artifact.6. ReleaseApprove and promote a known version.7. DeployPut infrastructure and application into an environment.8. Operate & MonitorRun, observe, support and improve the service.

What you should be able to do

  • Explain why DevSecOps is DevOps with integrated security.
  • Add basic threat/security requirements.
  • Run secret/SAST/dependency/IaC/container/DAST checks.
  • Generate an SBOM.
  • Use least privilege and a secrets manager.
  • Collect security-relevant logs.

Hands-on project for this level

Secure TaskPulse Lite: the beginner DevOps lab plus basic security checks.

  1. Add authentication/authorization requirement.
  2. Enable secret scanning and Sonar-style checks.
  3. Run Trivy/Checkov and ZAP baseline.
  4. Generate an SBOM.
  5. Use a secrets manager and least-privilege deployment identity.
1
STAGE 1

Plan

Think about security before writing code.

Key activities
  • Write normal requirements.
  • Add simple security requirements.
  • Ask what data is sensitive and who can access it.
  • Draw a basic trust boundary.
Tools and how they are used
  • Jira — track functional and security acceptance criteria
  • Confluence — record simple threat notes
  • Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool or simple diagram — identify user, API, database and trust boundaries
What leaves the stage
  • User story
  • Security acceptance criteria
  • Basic threat model
Security built into this stage
  • Identify authentication, authorization and sensitive data requirements.
  • Create security work items before code exists.
TaskPulse example

Add criteria: only authenticated users can see their own tasks; passwords/tokens are never logged.

2
STAGE 2

Code

Prevent obvious security mistakes while coding.

Key activities
  • Review code.
  • Do not commit secrets.
  • Validate input.
  • Use maintained dependencies.
Tools and how they are used
  • GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket — review every change
  • SonarLint — show code quality/security issues in the IDE
  • pre-commit hooks — run linters and secret checks locally
  • secret scanner — detect keys/tokens before merge
What leaves the stage
  • Reviewed code
  • No known committed secret
  • Developer scan results
Security built into this stage
  • Secure coding
  • Pre-commit secret detection
  • Peer review of authorization logic.
TaskPulse example

The API validates task titles, authorization checks owner_id, and a pre-commit secret scan blocks accidental cloud keys.

3
STAGE 3

Build

Build in CI and inspect dependencies/code.

Key activities
  • Build from lock files.
  • Run static analysis.
  • Run software composition/dependency scan.
Tools and how they are used
  • SonarQube — server-side static analysis and quality gate
  • SCA tool / dependency scanner — find vulnerable third-party libraries
  • CI runner — run scans on each merge
What leaves the stage
  • Build output
  • SAST result
  • Dependency vulnerability report
Security built into this stage
  • SAST
  • SCA
  • License checks where required.
TaskPulse example

CI blocks a merge if a newly introduced critical dependency vulnerability has no accepted exception.

4
STAGE 4

Test

Test the running application for security as well as correctness.

Key activities
  • Unit/integration tests.
  • Basic DAST against a test environment.
  • Scan Terraform/Kubernetes configuration.
Tools and how they are used
  • PyTest/JUnit — functional tests
  • OWASP ZAP — baseline DAST against the test API/UI
  • Checkov or Trivy config — scan Terraform/Kubernetes/IaC
What leaves the stage
  • Functional test report
  • DAST report
  • IaC scan report
Security built into this stage
  • SAST/DAST results treated as defects.
  • IaC security check before infrastructure changes.
TaskPulse example

A temporary test instance is started; ZAP baseline checks common web weaknesses and Checkov scans Terraform.

5
STAGE 5

Package

Scan the deployable artifact and describe what is inside it.

Key activities
  • Build image.
  • Scan image.
  • Generate SBOM.
  • Push immutable artifact.
Tools and how they are used
  • Docker/BuildKit — build OCI image
  • Trivy/Grype — scan OS and language packages in the image
  • Syft — generate an SBOM
  • Registry — store immutable image
What leaves the stage
  • Container image
  • Vulnerability report
  • SBOM
Security built into this stage
  • Container vulnerability scan
  • SBOM creation.
TaskPulse example

taskpulse-api image is scanned; its CycloneDX/SPDX SBOM is stored with the release.

6
STAGE 6

Release

Check policy before promoting.

DevSecOps gate sequence

PLAN       threat model + security acceptance criteria
CODE       review + SAST/secret checks
BUILD      SAST/SCA + controlled dependency sources
TEST       unit/integration + DAST + IaC/Kubernetes scans
PACKAGE    image scan + SBOM + signature/provenance
RELEASE    verify + policy-as-code + risk exception check
DEPLOY     least privilege + admission/runtime policy + secret references
OPERATE    SIEM/runtime detection + vulnerability/audit feedback

The important concept is not “run every scanner.” It is to place the highest-signal control at the earliest useful point, then carry evidence forward so production does not need to rediscover what the artifact contains.

DevOpsDevSecOps

What actually changes?

DevSecOps does not replace the DevOps pipeline. It adds security responsibilities, evidence and enforceable policy to the same software-delivery path.

DimensionDevOpsDevSecOps
Primary goalFast, repeatable delivery and reliable operation.Fast, repeatable delivery with security/risk controls embedded in the same path.
Security timingOften performed as separate reviews or platform controls.Security activities occur in Plan, Code, Build, Test, Package, Release, Deploy and Operate.
Build outputVersioned binary/image.Versioned binary/image + vulnerability/SBOM/signature/provenance evidence as maturity increases.
Release gateTests, approval, deployment policy.Tests + vulnerability policy + signature/provenance + IaC/admission/compliance policy.
RuntimeReliability, capacity, incidents.Reliability + detection/response + audit + vulnerability posture.
Team modelDevelopers + operations/platform/SRE.Same teams plus security engineering/AppSec/SOC capabilities integrated through paved-road automation.

Infrastructure provisioning + application deployment by target

A common beginner mistake is to treat “deployment” as one technology. The target dictates the deployment mechanism. Terraform primarily creates platform resources; the application delivery tool depends on the target.

TargetExamplesInfrastructure provisioningApplication deploymentUse when
Virtual machinesAWS EC2, Azure VM/VMSS, GCE, VMware, OpenStackTerraform provisions network, VM/scale set, disks, LB, IAM and DNS.Ansible installs runtime or pulls a signed artifact/image. Immutable option: Packer creates a golden image and the scale group rolls to it.Best when legacy middleware, OS-level control or non-container workloads are required.
Managed KubernetesEKS, AKS, GKETerraform provisions cluster, node pools, VPC/VNet, IAM/workload identity, load balancer integration and registry access.Helm/Kustomize deploy; Argo CD can reconcile from Git.Good for many containerized services with standardized platform needs.
On-prem KubernetesOpenShift, Rancher-managed, vanilla KubernetesTerraform may provision VMware/OpenStack/network/DNS; cluster bootstrap may use platform-specific automation.Helm/Kustomize + Argo CD works the same conceptually; private registry and on-prem storage/ingress are common.You own more cluster lifecycle, PKI, storage, network and capacity responsibilities.
Serverless functionsAWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud FunctionsTerraform creates function, role/identity, event source/API, network integration, secrets and logging.Publish ZIP or container image; shift alias/version or deploy a new revision.Good for event-driven or short request handlers. Watch runtime limits, cold starts, concurrency and vendor integration.
Serverless containersAWS App Runner/Fargate, Azure Container Apps, Google Cloud RunTerraform creates service, identity, ingress, autoscaling, network connector and secrets.Point a new service revision to the immutable container digest.Good when you want containers without managing a cluster.
PaaS application serviceAzure App Service, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App EngineTerraform provisions app/environment, plan/instances, identity, network and configuration.Deploy package or image through platform slot/revision/rolling mechanism.Good for straightforward web applications where platform constraints are acceptable.
Static frontendS3 + CloudFront, Azure Static Web Apps/Storage, GCS + CDNTerraform creates storage, CDN, DNS, TLS, access policies and optional WAF.Upload versioned frontend bundle and use cache-busting/invalidation.Simple, cheap and scalable for browser-only assets.
Bare metal / traditional middlewarePhysical Linux/Windows, app serversTerraform may integrate with virtualization/IPAM/DNS; PXE/vendor tooling can provision hosts.Ansible installs middleware, certificates, agents and application binaries.Appropriate for constraints that prevent cloud-native patterns; operational overhead is highest.

VM mental model

Terraform creates the machine. Ansible configures/deploys to the machine. You may deploy a binary, systemd service, container or baked image.

Kubernetes mental model

Terraform creates the cluster/platform. Helm/Kustomize defines the workload. Argo CD can continuously reconcile the workload from Git.

Serverless mental model

Terraform creates the function/service and its identity/network/events. The release updates a package, container digest, alias or revision. There is usually no Ansible.

Tool glossary — what each tool actually does

Tools are grouped by responsibility. Organizations can substitute equivalent products; understanding the responsibility matters more than memorizing brands.

ToolCategoryWhat it does / how it fits
JiraPlanning / work managementBacklog, user stories, defects, security findings, exceptions and release scope. It does not build or deploy anything; it provides ownership and traceability.
ConfluenceDocumentationArchitecture notes, ADRs, runbooks, threat models, operating procedures and release documentation.
GitHub / GitLab / BitbucketSource control platformHosts Git repositories, pull/merge requests, protected branches, reviews, status checks and often CI/CD.
JenkinsCI/CD orchestrationRuns pipelines on agents, stages jobs, integrates scanners, stores build metadata and performs deployments. Requires plugin/credential hygiene.
GitHub ActionsCI/CD orchestrationRepository-native workflows. Commonly uses OIDC to obtain short-lived cloud credentials.
GitLab CICI/CD orchestrationPipeline-as-code, runners, environments, artifacts, security scanning integrations and deployment workflows.
SonarLintDeveloper static analysisIDE feedback while coding. Helps catch code smells, bugs and some security issues before commit.
SonarQubeCentral static analysisServer-side code quality/SAST analysis with quality gates, history and project reporting.
Maven / GradleJava build toolsResolve dependencies, compile, test and package Java/JVM applications.
npm / yarnJavaScript package/build toolsInstall locked dependencies and run frontend build/test scripts.
JUnit / PyTestUnit/integration test frameworksRun repeatable automated tests and emit test results for CI.
OWASP ZAPDASTScans a running web application/API for common security weaknesses. Best run against an authorized test environment.
TrivySecurity scannerScans container images, filesystems, dependencies, IaC/Kubernetes config and can generate SBOMs.
GrypeVulnerability scannerScans container images/filesystems/SBOMs for known package vulnerabilities.
CheckovIaC scannerChecks Terraform, Kubernetes and other IaC for misconfigurations and policy violations.
Docker / BuildKitContainer buildBuilds OCI container images. BuildKit adds better caching, multi-stage builds, secrets mounts and modern build features.
SyftSBOM generatorCreates software bills of materials from images/filesystems in formats such as SPDX/CycloneDX.
Cosign / SigstoreArtifact signingSigns container images and attestations; supports verification of identity and provenance.
OPA / ConftestPolicy as codeEvaluates Rego policies against configuration such as Kubernetes, Terraform plans or JSON/YAML release metadata.
Argo CDKubernetes GitOpsContinuously reconciles Kubernetes desired state stored in Git with cluster state and reports drift/health.
TerraformInfrastructure as CodePlans and provisions cloud/on-prem resources through providers: networks, VMs, managed Kubernetes, IAM, databases, serverless and more.
AnsibleConfiguration managementConnects to hosts and idempotently configures OS packages, services, files, hardening and application rollout. Common for VM/bare-metal delivery.
HelmKubernetes packagingTemplates and versions Kubernetes application manifests as charts.
KustomizeKubernetes configurationApplies overlays/patches to Kubernetes YAML without a templating language; useful for environment differences.
PrometheusMetricsScrapes or receives time-series metrics; widely used for Kubernetes and application observability.
GrafanaDashboards / alertingVisualizes metrics/logs/traces and can manage alerts depending on deployment.
Elastic / ELKLogs / searchCentralizes and indexes logs for troubleshooting, dashboards, detection and audit use cases.
SplunkLogs / SIEMSearch, analytics and security monitoring over machine data; often used for enterprise operations/SOC workflows.
Vault / Cloud Secrets ManagerSecretsStores, rotates and audits secrets. Prefer short-lived/dynamic credentials and workload identity over copying secrets into CI.
ECR / ACR / Artifact RegistryContainer registryStores OCI images with IAM/RBAC, lifecycle and scanning/integration features.
Nexus / ArtifactoryArtifact repositoryStores and proxies packages/binaries; supports promotion and controlled dependency sources.

One complete TaskPulse walk-through aligned to the diagram

Use this as the “story” that ties all six views together.

StageTaskPulse walkthrough
1. PlanCreate TP-1, architecture sketch, acceptance criteria and target environments. In DevSecOps also add auth/data-security acceptance criteria and a lightweight threat model.
2. CodeFeature branch/PR changes React + FastAPI. Review before merge. DevSecOps adds secret/SAST checks and risk-sensitive CODEOWNERS.
3. BuildCI restores locked dependencies and builds frontend/API. DevSecOps adds SAST/SCA and hardened build identity.
4. TestRun unit + integration + smoke tests. DevSecOps adds DAST, IaC/Kubernetes config scan and security regression tests.
5. PackageBuild taskpulse-api OCI image and frontend bundle. DevSecOps scans image, generates SBOM and signs/attests the artifact.
6. ReleaseSelect the already-tested digest for staging/prod. DevSecOps verifies signature/provenance and evaluates policy/exception state.
7. DeployTerraform provisions target; Ansible deploys VM, Helm/Argo CD deploy Kubernetes, provider revision/alias deploys serverless. Secure identities/secrets are target-specific.
8. OperatePrometheus/Grafana + logs show version, errors and latency. DevSecOps also routes audit/detection/vulnerability signals to SIEM/SOC and back to backlog.

Concrete target examples

VM

  1. Terraform: VPC/subnet/security group/EC2/LB/IAM.
  2. Ansible: OS packages, runtime, monitoring agent, service config.
  3. Deploy signed/versioned artifact.
  4. Health check then load-balancer traffic.

Kubernetes

  1. Terraform: EKS/AKS/GKE or underlying on-prem infrastructure.
  2. Helm/Kustomize: Deployment, Service, Ingress, Config, NetworkPolicy.
  3. Argo CD: sync desired Git state.
  4. Observe rollout and rollback by digest.

Serverless

  1. Terraform: function/service, role/identity, API/events, secrets and logs.
  2. Publish ZIP or OCI image.
  3. Promote alias/revision or weighted traffic.
  4. Monitor native metrics plus application telemetry.

Practical learning roadmap

Beginner — build confidence

  1. Linux basics + Git.
  2. One scripting language.
  3. Docker basics.
  4. One CI platform.
  5. Terraform fundamentals.
  6. Deploy to one VM.
  7. Kubernetes basics.
  8. Basic monitoring.
  9. For DevSecOps: secrets, SAST/SCA, container/IaC scan.

Intermediate — build repeatability

  1. Reusable pipelines.
  2. Multi-environment IaC.
  3. Ansible + Helm.
  4. Artifact repositories and promotion.
  5. Integration/performance testing.
  6. GitOps and rollback.
  7. For DevSecOps: threat modeling, DAST, SBOM/signing, policy-as-code.

Advanced — build platforms

  1. Platform engineering and paved roads.
  2. SRE/SLO/error budgets.
  3. Progressive delivery.
  4. Hybrid/multi-region architecture.
  5. Supply-chain provenance.
  6. Workload identity and policy enforcement.
  7. Continuous controls and DORA metrics.
Suggested progression
Do not begin by installing 25 tools. Pick one CI platform, one cloud or lab environment and one example application. Add capabilities in the order they appear in the pipeline. The advanced sections then become architecture choices rather than a list of unfamiliar products.

Common questions

Do I need Jenkins, GitHub Actions and GitLab CI together?
No. Choose one CI/CD orchestrator unless you have an explicit integration or migration reason. The diagram lists examples, not mandatory simultaneous components.
Do I always need Ansible if I use Terraform?
No. Terraform provisions resources. Ansible is especially useful when you must configure mutable VMs or bare-metal hosts. Kubernetes and serverless deployments typically use different mechanisms.
Should Terraform deploy application versions?
It can, especially for serverless or tightly coupled platform resources, but many teams separate slower infrastructure lifecycle from frequent application releases. The important rule is that the selected artifact version is immutable and traceable.
Is DevSecOps just adding scanners?
No. Scanners are only one part. DevSecOps also includes threat/risk decisions, identity, secrets, policy, artifact integrity, secure infrastructure defaults, runtime detection, audit evidence and managed exceptions.
Which target should a beginner learn first?
A single Linux VM is the clearest place to learn networking, processes and deployment. Then learn containers and Kubernetes. Serverless is operationally simpler but can hide some fundamentals, so it is best learned alongside rather than instead of the basics.
